label: Protozoa by How They Move
rows: Amebas (ameboid)
Pseudopods: the trophozoite crawls; the cyst is nonmotile (slide 16)
Entamoeba histolytica, Naegleria fowleri, Acanthamoeba
Ciliate
Cilia fringe the trophozoite (slide 34)
Balantidium coli, “an intestinal ciliate” (slide 33): the only one
Flagellates
Flagella; Trichomonas adds an undulating membrane (slide 36)
Trichomonas vaginalis, Giardia lamblia; the hemoflagellates Trypanosoma brucei, Trypanosoma cruzi, Leishmania (slide 42)
Apicomplexans (sporozoans)
No locomotor organelles in the trophozoite; carried by arthropod vectors, food, water or other means (slide 55)
Plasmodium, Toxoplasma, Cryptosporidium (slide 55); the coccidians Toxoplasma, Sarcocystis, Cryptosporidium, Isospora, Cyclospora, Babesia (slide 63)

key: apicomplexans: no locomotor organelles, so they ride vectors, food or water
mnemonic.breaks: Naegleria is an ameba, but slide 25’s picture also shows it in a flagellated stage.

label: The Three Amebas Side by Side
rows: Entamoeba histolytica
Humans are the primary hosts; tropical countries; polluted water supplies (prisons, hospitals, juvenile care institutions)
Cysts swallowed: the fecal-oral route; sometimes sexually transmitted
Amebiasis, 90% asymptomatic: intestinal (dysentery; cecum, appendix, colon, rectum) or extraintestinal (liver abscess: amebic hepatitis)
Naegleria fowleri
Standing water with a high bacterial count: hot springs, lakes, streams, unchlorinated pools; Florida’s freshwater lakes
Nasal contact with water (diving, waterskiing, sinus rinsing even with tap water); up the olfactory nerve
Primary amebic meningoencephalitis (slide 29: “primary acute”): mostly children and young adults; death in 3–7 days
Acanthamoeba
Worldwide: freshwater lakes, hot tubs, swimming pools
The eye (contact lens wearers); a break in the skin or the nasal passages
Amebic keratitis (does not typically disseminate); granulomatous amebic encephalitis: meningitis symptoms, longer progression, survival only 2–3%

rows.note: ★ Entamoeba: water treatment is the best prevention (a vaccine is under development). ★ Naegleria: treatment must be early. Naegleria prevention: no swimming or diving in unchlorinated water; nose plugs.
Slide 4’s summary table pairs Acanthamoeba’s contact lenses with granulomatous amebic encephalitis; slides 31–32 put the contact lens with the keratitis, and the skin or nose with the encephalitis.

mnemonic.hook: Entamoeba is Eaten, Naegleria goes up the Nose, Acanthamoeba gets in your eye (the lens).
key: Entamoeba histolytica: swallowed cysts, gut and liver
Naegleria fowleri: nasal water, brain in days
Acanthamoeba: contact lens keratitis; a slower brain infection
mnemonic.breaks: Acanthamoeba’s encephalitis enters through broken skin or the nose, not the eye; Entamoeba is sometimes sexually transmitted.

label: Giardia, Trichomonas and Balantidium
rows: Giardia lamblia
Flagellate: symmetrical heart shape, concave ventral surface that acts as a suction cup; small, compact, multinucleate cysts
Cysts in water and food; reservoirs beavers, cattle, coyotes, cats, humans; ★ the one you get camping (slide 4: common in campers)
Giardiasis: diarrhea, abdominal pain. Shed in feces intermittently, so microscopy is difficult: polymerase chain reaction. Killed by boiling, ozone, iodine
Trichomonas vaginalis
Flagellate: small, pear-shaped, 4 anterior flagella, undulating membrane; trophozoite only, no cyst
Human urogenital tract; sexually transmitted; a strict parasite that cannot survive long outside the host
Trichomoniasis: ★ one you will meet in clinical practice; the most common curable sexually transmitted disease in young, sexually active women. Vaginal smear
Balantidium coli
Ciliate
Cyst-containing food or water; lives in the intestines of pigs and cattle
Balantidiosis: persistent diarrhea, occasionally dysentery; healthy humans are resistant; rarely enters the blood

mnemonic.hook: Giardia goes camping, Trichomonas goes to bed, Balantidium lives on the farm.
key: Giardia: cysts in stream water and food, beavers
Trichomonas: sexually transmitted, no cyst, cannot survive long outside the host
Balantidium: pigs and cattle, cysts in food or water
mnemonic.breaks: Giardia’s reservoirs include cattle too; Balantidium is a ciliate, not a flagellate.

label: The Two Trypanosomes
cols: Vector and how it gets in
rows: Trypanosoma brucei
African sleeping sickness. Gambiense: West Africa, chronic (brain symptoms years later). Rhodesiense: East Africa, acute (brain symptoms within 3–4 weeks)
Tsetse fly; reservoir mammals. The bite inoculates the skin: primary chancre
Antigenic variation; spleen, lymph nodes, brain: sleep disturbances, seizures, coma. Seen in blood, spinal fluid, lymph nodes; card agglutination test
Trypanosoma cruzi
Chagas disease (American trypanosomiasis): Central and South America; ★ spreading into the Southern United States by vector migration
Reduviid (kissing) bug: its feces inoculated into a cutaneous portal. Also congenital, transfusion, organ transplant, contaminated food
Romaña’s sign (chagoma: eyelid swelling with conjunctivitis); masses of the parasite in heart muscle and large intestine; chronic heart and brain inflammation

rows.note: ★ Vector control is the best way to control both: eliminate the tsetse fly; control the reduviid bug. ★ Treatment must be early: Trypanosoma brucei before neurological involvement, Trypanosoma cruzi early.
★ The blood-smear picture (slides 5 and 46): wavy flagellates swimming between red blood cells. Know it as Trypanosoma.

mnemonic.hook: Brucei puts Africa to Bed with a Bite; Cruzi Crawls in and Clutches the heart.
key: Trypanosoma brucei: tsetse fly bite, sleeping sickness, Africa
Trypanosoma cruzi: kissing-bug feces into the skin, heart disease, the Americas
mnemonic.breaks: Trypanosoma cruzi also inflames the brain, and also spreads congenitally, by transfusion, transplant and food.

label: Vector-Borne Protozoa and Their Vectors
rows: Trypanosoma brucei (African sleeping sickness)
Tsetse fly
Primary chancre; sleep disturbances and coma once it reaches the brain
Trypanosoma cruzi (Chagas disease)
Reduviid (kissing) bug; Triatoma on slide 129
Romaña’s sign: eyelid swelling with conjunctivitis
Leishmania (leishmaniasis)
Female sand fly (needs a blood meal to make eggs); dogs are alternate hosts
Cutaneous sore (oriental sore, Baghdad boil); espundia; visceral, kala azar
Plasmodium (malaria)
Female Anopheles mosquito; also blood transfusion, mother to fetus
Chills-fever-sweating every 48–72 hours as red blood cells rupture; ring trophozoites in red blood cells
Babesia microti (babesiosis)
Blacklegged deer tick (hard ticks, slide 129)
Attacks red blood cells: hemolytic anemia; serious without a spleen. The first protozoan linked to a vector

rows.note: ★ Vector control is the best way to control the hemoflagellate diseases (tsetse fly, reduviid bug); for malaria, mosquito control is key (slide 61).

mnemonic.hook: The tsetse puts you to sleep, the kissing bug swells your eyelid, the sand fly leaves a sore, the mosquito sets fevers on a clock, the tick bursts red cells.
mnemonic.breaks: The kissing bug infects through its feces, not its bite; Leishmania’s most severe form is visceral (kala azar), not the sore; Plasmodium bursts red cells too.

label: The Three Forms of Leishmaniasis
rows: Cutaneous: oriental sore, Baghdad boil
A localized ulcerated sore
Espundia
Skin and mucous membrane infection of the head; a chronic infection that occurs after the cutaneous form
Systemic (visceral)
High intermittent fever; weight loss; enlarged spleen, liver and lymph nodes. Kala azar is the most severe form, fatal if untreated

rows.note: Slide 52: if the infected macrophage does not migrate, the infection stays localized; if it migrates, it becomes systemic. Slide 53: co-infection with malaria is an increasing issue and may make diagnosis difficult.

key: espundia: skin and mucous membranes of the head, after the skin sore
systemic (visceral): enlarged spleen, liver, lymph nodes; kala azar the worst
mnemonic.breaks: “Snout” stands for the whole head’s skin and mucous membranes, not only the nose.

label: Malaria’s Phases: Human, Then Mosquito
rows: Exoerythrocytic (asexual)
Human: liver
The infected female mosquito injects sporozoites; they localize in the liver and undergo schizogony, releasing numerous merozoites into the circulation in 5–16 days
Erythrocytic (asexual)
Human: red blood cells
Merozoites enter red blood cells, become circular ring trophozoites and multiply; the cell bursts, releasing merozoites (symptoms come as cells rupture, slide 60)
Gametocytic
Human: blood
Merozoites differentiate into gametes, now in the human’s blood
Sexual
Female Anopheles mosquito
The mosquito draws infected red blood cells; gametes fertilize into a diploid cell that forms sporozoites in its stomach; the sporozoites lodge in the salivary glands

mnemonic.hook: Liver, Ring, Gamete, Mosquito: the parasite checks into the Liver, Rings the red cells, pairs up as Gametes, and flies home in the Mosquito.
key: erythrocytic: ring trophozoites, red cells burst
gametocytic: gametes in the human’s blood
sexual phase: fertilization, sporozoites to the salivary glands
mnemonic.breaks: Slide 59’s figure says gametocytes where slide 58 says gametes; the 5–16 days is merozoites reaching the blood, not the 10–16 day incubation (slide 60).

label: The Coccidians: Source and Who Is at Risk
cols: Who is at risk, and the disease
rows: Toxoplasma gondii
Raw meat, or substances contaminated by cat feces (cats harbor the oocysts); transplacental (33%)
Pregnant women: spontaneous abortion, stillbirth, hydrocephalus, intracranial calcifications, chorioretinitis. Immunocompromised: toxoplasma encephalitis. Most cases go unnoticed
Sarcocystis
Undercooked meat: Sarcocystis hominis (cattle), Sarcocystis suihominis (pigs)
Diarrhea, nausea, abdominal pain; other species: muscle cysts, myalgia, weakness, edema
Cryptosporidium
Recreational water (tolerates pool chlorine), contaminated water, ice, food; infectious dose as little as 10
Acquired immunodeficiency syndrome and other immunocompromised: chronic persistent diarrhea; young children and the elderly likely infected. Gastroenteritis
Isospora belli
Fecally contaminated food or drink
Primarily immunocompromised hosts; usually asymptomatic or self-limited; diarrhea, fatty stools
Cyclospora cayetanensis
Oral-fecal: fresh produce and water (the 2026 iceberg lettuce outbreak)
Watery diarrhea, cramps, bloating, fever; multiple stool samples; acid-fast stain

rows.note: Babesia, the sixth coccidian on slide 63, comes by tick: see the vector table above.

mnemonic.hook: Cat box, Steak, Swimming pool, Immune system, Salad.
key: Toxoplasma: cat feces (and raw meat, and the placenta)
mnemonic.breaks: Cryptosporidium also hits the immunocompromised hardest; Toxoplasma also comes from raw meat, so “Steak” fits it too.

label: The Four Helminth Life Cycles
cols: How it gets in, and where it goes
rows: A
The human swallows the mature egg in food or water; larvae hatch and burrow, may pass lungs → pharynx → swallowed; adults reproduce in the intestine; eggs leave in feces
Ascaris lumbricoides, Trichuris trichiura; Taenia saginata is “Cycle C and modified A”
B
Infective larvae in soil penetrate the skin; lungs → pharynx → swallowed; adults reproduce in the intestine; eggs reach the soil in feces
The hookworms (Necator americanus, Ancylostoma duodenale), Strongyloides stercoralis
C
The human eats the encysted worm in muscle (undercooked meat); gastric passage frees the larva; a food animal grazing on fecally contaminated grass carries the cysts
Trichinella spiralis; the tapeworms Taenia saginata and Taenia solium
D
Involves an intermediate host: larvae penetrate the skin or are eaten; intermediate hosts release infective larvae into water or, if they are biting insects, transmit through the bite
Wuchereria bancrofti, Onchocerca volvulus, Loa loa, Schistosoma, Opisthorchis sinensis, Paragonimus westermani

rows.note: ★ Adulthood and mating occur in the definitive host (starred on slide 79); larval development occurs in the intermediate host; a transport (paratenic) host allows no development.
The slides give no cycle letter for Enterobius, Angiostrongylus, Toxocara, Dirofilaria, Fasciola or Echinococcus. Trichinella’s own cycle (slide 102) releases no eggs.

mnemonic.hook: A = Ate the egg, B = Barefoot larvae, C = Cyst in meat, D = Detour through an intermediate host.
key: Cycle B: larvae through the skin (hookworms, Strongyloides)
Cycle C: encysted larvae in undercooked meat (Trichinella, Taenia)
Cycle D: an intermediate host (the filarial worms, the flukes)
mnemonic.breaks: Cycle D larvae can also enter through the skin (Schistosoma) or a bite (the filarial worms), so skin entry is not Cycle B alone.

label: Intestinal Nematodes: Swallowed as Eggs or Entered as Larvae
rows: Trichuris trichiura (whipworm)
Egg: fecal pollution of soil with eggs; humans the sole host
Pierces capillaries: localized hemorrhage; heavy loads, dysentery and rectal prolapse
Ascaris lumbricoides (roundworm)
Egg: in food, drink or contaminated objects
Lung migration: eosinophilic pneumonitis; heavy loads, intestinal obstruction; worms do not attach
Enterobius vermicularis (pinworm)
Egg: close contact and fomites; self-inoculation
★ Most common worm disease of children in temperate zones; anal itching; tape test
Necator americanus, Ancylostoma duodenale (hookworms)
Larva: filariform larvae burrow into the skin of bare feet
Pneumonia, bloody diarrhea; significant blood loss: anemia
Strongyloides stercoralis (threadworm)
Larva: penetrates the skin; can reinfect the same host without leaving the body
Pneumonitis, eosinophilia, bloody diarrhea, malabsorption
Trichinella spiralis (trichina worm)
Larva: in undercooked pork or bear meat
Cysts in muscle, heart, brain: muscle and joint pain, pronounced eosinophilia, myocarditis

rows.note: Table 23.4 (slide 84) also gives “fecal pollution of soil with eggs” for the hookworms and Strongyloides: feces put the eggs in the soil, and the larva that hatches is the infective stage.

mnemonic.hook: Swallow the Whip, the Ball and the Pin as eggs; the Hook and the Thread crawl in barefoot; the Trichina waits in the pork.
key: Necator and Ancylostoma, the hookworms: larva through the skin
Strongyloides, the threadworm: larva through the skin
mnemonic.breaks: Trichinella is eaten, not barefoot. Angiostrongylus (eaten in snails; eosinophilic meningitis) is not on Table 23.4.

label: Tissue Nematodes and Their Vectors
rows: Wuchereria bancrofti
Mosquitoes (Anopheles/Culex, slide 129)
Lymphatics
Bancroftian filariasis: lymphatic blockage, elephantiasis (massive swelling of the extremities)
Onchocerca volvulus
Black flies
Subcutaneous tissue; adult females migrate to the eyes
River blindness: antigens of Wolbachia, its bacterial endosymbiont, inflame cornea, retina, optic nerve
Loa loa
Small flies (mangrove or deer flies)
Around and under the skin; may enter the eye
African eye worm; temperature-sensitive

rows.note: All three are filarial worms: Life Cycle D with the vector as intermediate host; chronic, deforming disease. Dirofilaria is also a vector-borne filarial worm: heartworm in dogs; in humans, lung coin lesions mistaken for malignancy, and skin nodules.

mnemonic.hook: The mosquito swells the legs, the black fly blacks out the eyes, and Loa loa crawls across the eye: “look, look”.
key: Loa loa: the eye worm under the skin
mnemonic.breaks: Both Onchocerca and Loa loa reach the eye; river blindness is the one tied to Wolbachia bacteria.

label: The Flukes: Every One Needs a Snail
cols: Where it lives, what it does
rows: Schistosoma (blood flukes)
Humans and freshwater snails
Cercariae penetrate the skin in water where the snail lives (slides 8, 112–114); Table 23.4: ingestion of fresh water containing larval stage
Liver, then adults migrate to the intestine or bladder and feed on blood; eggs in urine and feces; itchy entry site. Prevention: snail control
Opisthorchis sinensis (Chinese liver fluke)
Mammals, snails, fish
Inadequately cooked fish (slide 8: “don’t eat freshwater sushi”)
Bile duct
Fasciola hepatica (sheep liver fluke)
Herbivores, snails, aquatic plants
Raw aquatic plants (Table 23.4: water and water plants)
Liver; chronic phase: blocked bile duct, gall bladder or pancreas
Paragonimus westermani (Oriental lung fluke)
Carnivorous animals, snails, crustaceans
Undercooked crustaceans (crabs)
Lungs: cough, pleural pain, abscess

rows.note: Where the slides disagree: Table 23.4 says people get Schistosoma by ingesting fresh water that contains the larval stage; slides 8 and 112–114 say the larva penetrates the skin. Know both.

mnemonic.hook: Every fluke needs a snail; then Swim, Sushi, Salad, Shellfish.
key: Schistosoma: larvae through the skin in snail water
mnemonic.breaks: Table 23.4 has Schistosoma swallowed, not swum; “Salad” means raw aquatic plants only.

label: The Tapeworms: What Is Eaten, What It Causes
rows: Taenia saginata (beef tapeworm)
Humans definitive; cattle intermediate
Raw or undercooked beef with encysted larvae
Taeniasis: few symptoms, vague abdominal pain, nausea; proglottids in the stool
Taenia solium (pork tapeworm)
Humans definitive; swine intermediate
Undercooked pork: taeniasis. Embryonated eggs in food or water: cysticercosis
Cysticercosis: larvae encyst in all tissues; most damaging in heart muscle, eye, brain (seizures, psychiatric disturbances)
Echinococcus
Dogs definitive (alveolar form: foxes, coyotes, dogs); sheep, cattle, goats, pigs intermediate
From handling infected dogs
Cystic (hydatid disease): slowly enlarging cysts in liver and lungs. Alveolar: parasitic tumors in lungs, liver, brain

rows.note: Slide 8 says Taenia saginata “causes weight loss and wasting in host”; slide 119 says few symptoms. Slide 118 says humans are the definitive host and animals intermediate; slide 124 gives dogs as the definitive host of Echinococcus, and slide 121 has Taenia solium larvae encysting in human tissues after swallowed eggs.

mnemonic.hook: Beef is Bland, Pork goes to the Brain, the Dog gives hyDatid cysts.
key: Taenia saginata: few symptoms, proglottids in stool
Taenia solium: swallowed eggs, cysticercosis in brain, eye, heart
Echinococcus: from dogs, hydatid cysts in liver and lungs
mnemonic.breaks: Pork meat gives only intestinal taeniasis; it is the swallowed EGGS that reach the brain.

label: The Arthropod Vectors
rows: Mosquitoes
Need an aquatic habitat; females take the blood meal
Malaria, filariasis, dengue fever
Fleas
Highly motile, flattened bodies; feed on warm-blooded animals; carry zoonoses
Plague, murine typhus
Lice
Small, soft; attach to head and body hair; release feces that contaminate the wound
Epidemic typhus, relapsing fever
Hard (ixodid) ticks
Small, compact, rigid bodies
Bacterial, rickettsial and viral diseases (slide 129 adds Rocky Mountain spotted fever, Lyme disease, babesiosis)
Soft (argasid) ticks
Flexible outer bodies
Relapsing fever

rows.note: All ticks cling to vegetation and attach to the host on contact; larvae, nymphs and adults all take blood. Slide 129 (Table 23.6) vectors of this lecture’s parasites: Anopheles (malaria), Anopheles/Culex (filariasis), tsetse (African trypanosomiasis), sand fly (leishmaniasis), black fly (onchocerciasis), Triatoma (Chagas disease), hard ticks (babesiosis).

key: mosquitoes: aquatic habitat; malaria, filariasis, dengue
fleas: highly motile; plague, murine typhus
lice: live in head and body hair; epidemic typhus, relapsing fever
ixodid ticks: rigid; bacterial, rickettsial, viral diseases
mnemonic.breaks: Relapsing fever comes from both lice and soft ticks. “Jumpy” is a stand-in: slide 130 says only highly motile.
